newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - US in focus, fireworks seen elsewhere.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - US in focus, fireworks seen elsewhere.

text.p: The United States is the focus for major economic news events next week, but analysts said on Friday the threat of fireworks on financial markets extended not least to peripheral European countries.
"Bond, currency and equities markets could be very volatile next week -- there is so much potential for surprise and markets are in that kind of mood," said HSBC James Capel's Robert Prior.
Prior said markets would look especially closely at the Federal Open Market Committee's (FOMC) two-day meeting starting on Tuesday and then at the January non-farm payrolls on Friday.

The FOMC, policy-making arm of the Federal Reserve, was likely to keep interest rates steady, said Prior, a European economist at HSBC. He added markets might then assume, possibly wrongly, that it had advance hints about the payrolls number.
"Then if the payrolls rise is any higher than about 210,000, markets could turn jittery as to whether the Fed made the right decision. This could cause a nasty shock," Prior said.

Attention in the latter part of the week will also start to focus on another setpiece event, a Group of Seven (G7) meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors from leading industrialised nations in Berlin on the Saturday.
Prior said currency markets especially would be looking closely for the outcome of the Berlin talks for comments aimed at talking down the strength of the dollar.
"They will probably say there are happy with the level of the dollar but not want to see it go much further against the yen or the mark. That would be a trigger to sell the dollar."
However, Jan Loeys, global fixed income strategist at J.P. Morgan in London, said nothing important happened at six out of seven G7 finance ministers meetings.

"G7 countries do not need to wait for such meetings to discuss international coordination (of foreign exchange policy)," he said. "They can talk openly beforehand. We need to look at what central banks are saying in the meantime."
Loeys also underplayed the significance of the FOMC meeting, preferring to focus on high-yielding European bond markets which he was not alone in thinking were riding for a fall.

"We do not think anything will happen at the FOMC meeting," he said. "If it does it will trash U.S. Treasuries and Europe will follow, but not to the same extent -- though the Canadian market would get hurt."

Loeys said he would be watching the bilateral talks in Bonn on Friday between German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi in case of negative signals on European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

If Kohl was as tepid in his comments about the lira's chances of joining the first round of EMU as he was this week about Spain's prospects of doing so -- or worse still if he were silent on the issue -- this would reduce Italy's attraction.

"It would throw cold water on the lira and the short end of the Italian curve, though the long end seems quite protected," Loeys said. "It all depends where prices are on Friday morning because there has been so much selling off in the last three days so it might not be that negative."

Prior added a sceptical note about European high-yielders. "We have been bullish on the peripherals, but we may now be reaching a turning point in terms of spread convergence," he said, citing Italy, Spain and Sweden as ripe for selloffs.

Loeys said the Bundesbank council meeting on Thursday was unlikely to take any action on interest rates, leaving it for a subsequent meeting when there was more negative news on the economy to move to cut rates.
However, he said it was possible that Sweden might cut rates when the Riksbank meets, also on Thursday, since he said Sweden had been one of Europe's worst performing markets recently.

Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at Barclays de Zoete Wedd in London, said the Fed would probably keep interest rate policy on hold because this week's employment cost data had been reasonably encouraging.

On the G7, Reed said officials were reasonably happy with currencies where they were now. "But the Bundesbank is probably starting to get a bit concerned at the pace of mark weakness versus other ERM (European Exchange Rate Mechanism) currencies."
